itens.titulo: Context Engineering for Images: MIT researchers build VISTA, an agent harness that keeps images in memory for faster retrieval
itens.texto: Managing an agent’s context by storing all the input text it receives and giving it tools to search the text boosts its performance. For vision-language agents, the same is true of storing images. What’s new: Qiushi Han, Keya Hu, Linlu Qiu, and colleagues at MIT released VISTA , an agent that completed the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark of interactive visual-reasoning puzzles using 57.4 percent fewer actions than humans who had not encountered them before. The VISTA harness is freely available under the MIT license. Key insight: Given an image frame from a videogame or other interactive environment, agentic systems typically embed it and keep the embedding until the context is full, at which point they delete it. This raises two issues: Embeddings are lossy and may not retain valuable information, and once an embedding has been deleted, the model no longer has access to information it contained. Storing all frames in a persistent memory retains all the information they carry, and enabling an agent to retrieve and zoom in on them makes it possible to embed details that otherwise may not have been captured. How it works: VISTA works with Anthropic Claude Opus 5.0 or OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol. Its harness works similarly to other popular harnesses, except it retains all input frames and includes a tool that retrieves frames. Given a new frame and list of available keyboard actions (such as left, right, up, down, spacebar, or click), the agent tells the model to decide whether to (i) read or update notes, (ii) retrieve previous frames, (iii) retrieve previous actions and their results, or (iv) execute an action. It repeats this choice until the model takes action. After the environment updates (during which it may produce a series of frames), it adds to the model’s input the last frame and a new list of available actions and executes the loop again. The agent maintains two notes: information it deduces about the environment that can be reused across levels or sessions (for example, the difference between a brown block and a black background), and information deduced about the level or problem at hand (for example, that the character currently has a power-up or conditions under which the model failed previously). The agent decides when to read these notes. When the agent decides to retrieve earlier frames, the tool enables it to retrieve any number of frames and zoom in to any part of a frame. During an attempt to complete a puzzle or game level, VISTA stores in memory not only images but also a list of actions and their results. It can decide to retrieve any set of previous actions or summaries of all previous attempts. Results: The authors tested VISTA on ARC-AGI-3 (25 games), GameWorld (170 tasks in 34 games), and AI GameStore (10 games). It enabled Claude Opus 5.0 and GPT-5.6 Sol to outperform earlier agents as well as humans who encountered the same challenges for the first time. On ARC-AGI-3, VISTA with Claude Opus 5.0 achieved a perfect score of 100 Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE), meaning it completed all puzzles in fewer actions than first-time human players. (Earlier projects that achieved perfect RHAE scores, such as Tycho , generated programs that simulated the environments.) VISTA with GPT-5.6 Sol achieved 99 RHAE. Denied the ability to store frames, VISTA with GPT-5.6 Sol achieved 70 RHAE, which shows that the frames were useful. On GameWorld, VISTA with GPT-5.6 Sol completed 63.3 percent of tasks on average. First-time human players completed 55.3 percent, and the native harness with GPT-5.6 Sol completed 40 percent. On AI GameStore, VISTA with GPT-5.6 Sol achieved a much higher score than first-time players and the native harness, 40 percent better than humans on average. Why it matters: Games and other interactive environments generate potentially endless streams of frames, each of which contain information an agent may not have deduced earlier. Only so many frames fit in its context, and not all frames are relevant at any given moment. By storing all frames and giving the agent tools to retrieve them, agents can find the relevant frames and re-examine them within the current context. We're thinking: Apparently context engineering helps whether the medium is text or images. Multimodal systems benefit from multimodal context management.

itens.titulo: World Models Become Robot Playgrounds: Google Genie 4 combines with Gemini models to build better video game worlds, robotics training
itens.texto: Google says that Genie 4, its latest world model, will be used in tandem with Gemini models to create digital practice spaces for robots, giving them endless worlds to train in. So far, though, Google’s demos suggest there’s still a long way to go. What’s new : On October 27, Google announced Genie 4 , which it has released to a limited group of testers in a research preview. Genie 4 produces interactive worlds that Google says are even more realistic than its predecessor, Genie 3. Users can change a scene midway through with a text prompt, but now Gemini models help work those changes into the scene. Genie 4 also adds sound, which allows it to create real-time audio for each world it generates, whether it’s two people chatting on a motorcycle or snow crunching under a crowned crane’s feet. Google AI Ultra subscribers as well as some developers should be getting access in the weeks ahead. How it works: Genie 4 doesn’t have a technical report out yet, but Google’s announcement explains how Gemini models can help direct what Genie 4 renders. Navigation : Users move through a scene with video game-style mouse and keyboard controls. Text directions: While Genie 4 renders a scene, Gemini 3.8 Flash works alongside it as a director. It breaks the user’s goal into steps, then double-checks each new frame to make sure each of those steps has been executed, adjusting its plan if the user inserts changes as things go along. Video: Gemini Omni , Google’s video generation model, helps Genie 4 render more realistic scenery. Google demoed examples including a maple seed gracefully spinning and landing on grass, as well as people shuffling along a 1980s-era train platform. Robotics: In a demo, Google’s reasoning model Gemini 4 Argon broke a task into text-based steps for Genie 4 while it rendered a simulation of Apptronik’s Apollo humanoid robot playing checkers with a person. Google didn’t describe a robot control system in the loop. Results: Google’s announcement was full of curated demos, but the company didn’t offer any quantitative evaluations to back them up. Google says a simulation can run up to two minutes, roughly double Genie 3’s limit, but DeepMind research engineer Hang Qi noted that reaching that limit doesn’t guarantee that a scene will keep its consistency the whole time, according to Bloomberg . Google says it’s still working to improve complex physical interactions. One of its demos even includes a physics slip: A marble bust that drops onto a watermelon settles on its plinth when it should topple over the side. “There’s only so much that you can do with two minutes,” Google DeepMind product manager Diego Rivas said, per TechCrunch . “We’re still in the research journey. We’re not necessarily in the end product journey.” Behind the news: Genie 4 has plenty of company: The world models field is getting more crowded, although not every world model operates the same way. Like GWM Worlds 2 , the model Runway released in September, Genie 4 generates video in real time. Marble , from AI pioneer Fei-Fei Li’s startup World Labs, and HY-World 2.0 , an open-weights model from Chinese tech giant Tencent, build persistent 3D scenes instead. Robotics isn’t the only field disrupted by the new wave of world models. When Genie 3 opened to paying subscribers in January, it sparked a sharp selloff of video game stocks. In October, electric-vehicle maker Rivian bought world-model startup Third Dimension to bring self-driving simulation in house. The field is also consolidating. AMD agreed in September to buy World Labs for about $8.2 billion, and, per The Wall Street Journal , Amazon has been in talks to acquire Decart, whose products include world models for robotics and driving simulation. Genie 3 served as an environment for SIMA, DeepMind’s agent for 3D virtual worlds. Waymo later built a driving simulator on Genie 3 to generate unusual scenarios (things like a tornado or an elephant in the road). Runway has also pushed its world models toward robotics. In February it announced that robot-control policies acting inside a robotics version of its video model earned simulated scores that closely tracked their real-world results in tabletop tests. In September, Runway debuted a research preview of GWM Worlds 2 , a real-time world model with audio. It also announced Praxis-1 , a model for controlling real robots that it plans to release with open weights. Why it matters: Google’s clearest evidence that simulation can improve real robots comes from a different approach from other companies. A few weeks before Genie 4’s debut, Google showed Gemini 4 Argon writing physics simulations in the MuJoCo engine based on photos and video. From a single photo of a tabletop, Argon generated more than 4,500 practice episodes, and fine-tuning a robot-control model on them raised its real-world success rate from 56 percent to 75 percent. Google’s proposed path forward, which it calls hybrid world models, would combine elements of both the structured reasoning of language and code models with a generative model that renders pixels. Theoretically that could give generated environments reliable cause and effect, which is something video models often lack. We’re thinking: A good robot simulator lets plans fail, since robots learn from mistakes as well as successes. Genie 4 pairs its renderer up with a Gemini director that checks whether each step of a plan succeeded. This can accidentally drift the world toward whatever the intended outcome is. In the marble bust clip, the model itself seems to choose a neat landing on the plinth instead of the toppling over the side like physics says it should. Our question for DeepMind: Can a plan fail in Genie 4? We’d like to see that Apptronik robot hand mess up and drop a few checkers, too.

itens.titulo: Anthropic Opens Its Books: Anthropic's S-1 outlines company's strong financials, methods, potential risks after IPO
itens.texto: Claude’s maker will sell company shares to the public for the first time. Anthropic’s financial statements show first-half revenue that grew 14-fold from a year earlier, an operating profit in the second quarter, and hundreds of billions of dollars in commitments to buy computing power. What’s new: On October 26, Anthropic filed an S-1 , the registration statement a company must submit to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission before it goes public. Anthropic plans to list on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker ANT. According to the filing, the offering’s main purposes are to increase Anthropic’s capital and financial flexibility and to create a public market for its shares. Anthropic plans to use the money to support its continued growth, including much-needed compute and infrastructure. The offering: Anthropic could go public as soon as the week before Thanksgiving and hopes to sell roughly $100 billion in shares, according to The Wall Street Journal . The filing leaves the final share price and total share count blank. Some investors expect Anthropic’s post-IPO valuation to land between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion , according to Bloomberg . Who’s in charge: Public shareholders will get almost no say in the company’s future direction. A single share held by a company owned by Anthropic’s seven co-founders, including CEO Dario Amodei, carries 50.1 percent of the vote on most matters, and its voting power will automatically remain at 50.1 percent if Anthropic issues more stock. The numbers: Anthropic’s revenue is growing much faster than its spending, even accounting for the growing cost of compute. Revenue reached $16.3 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion a year earlier. Anthropic says it doesn’t expect revenue to keep growing quite that fast. In 2026’s second quarter, Anthropic earned an operating profit (revenue minus the costs of running the business) of $974 million on $11.6 billion in revenue, its first in any period the filing reports. The company’s quarterly compute and infrastructure expenses rose from $944 million in early 2025 to $5.6 billion in the second quarter of 2026, but compute and infrastructure’s share of revenue fell from 251 percent to 48 percent. Under standard accounting rules, Anthropic lost $80.7 billion in the first half of 2026, but most of that came from an accounting adjustment, not money the company spent. Day-to-day operations brought in $3.9 billion in cash. Anthropic has committed to spend hundreds of billions of dollars on computing power, often with companies that also finance it. Named deals include about $161.2 billion in rent on equipment from the chipmaker Broadcom, at least $114.5 billion with Google, at least $110 billion with Amazon, and up to $120.5 billion with SpaceXAI, under agreements that either party can cancel after early 2027. Google and Amazon both invested early in Anthropic, a relationship that the S-1 warns could lead to conflicts of interest. The S-1 reveals that Anthropic’s Claude wrote more than 90 percent of the contributions to Anthropic’s codebase in September 2026. However, the filing says that using AI to build more capable AI in this way “could also pose a considerable safety risk.” Risk disclosures: The S-1 laid out both conventional and unusual risks for a mainstream American technology company. Government sanctions could pose a future risk. In June 2026, the U.S. Department of Commerce imposed worldwide export restrictions on Fable 5 and Mythos 5, two configurations of what was then Anthropic’s most capable model. To comply, Anthropic switched off both models for every customer, while its other models stayed available. It restored them once Commerce lifted the restrictions. Disagreements with the Pentagon could cost Anthropic business, including with other government agencies and to companies that sell to the U.S. government. In February, after Anthropic said its technology shouldn’t be used for mass domestic surveillance or fully autonomous weapons, the President directed federal agencies to stop using it. The Department of Defense then designated Anthropic a supply-chain risk under two different laws. The final result of the dispute is still pending in court. Like other labs, security lapses during model testing expose the company to potential liabilities. During pre-release cybersecurity tests built by an outside partner, a setup error left models connected to the Internet. Four Anthropic models gained unauthorized access to real third-party computer systems. Anthropic found no evidence that any model pursued goals beyond its assigned task. It suspended some of those tests. The filing also notes concerns, raised inside Anthropic as well as by outside researchers and regulators, that sufficiently advanced AI could “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity” without appropriate safeguards. Why it matters: For developers using Claude, the filing should be more reassuring than alarming. Anthropic held $112.4 billion in cash at the end of June and turned an operating profit in the second quarter, which testifies to the company’s stability. Even export restrictions (the most direct hit to customers so far) proved temporary. Anthropic restored the models once the U.S. government lifted them and released updated versions in September. We’re thinking: Within just a few years, Anthropic has gone from a promising startup to potentially a trillion-dollar company. Stock valuations aside, Anthropic’s robust financials should help legitimate an industry that some critics have argued is overhyped. We’re less sure what to think about the filing’s risk factors: They’re a mix of sci-fi scenarios and genuine risks with implications that are difficult to forecast. We’re hopeful that public investment will help Anthropic continue to improve its products for years to come — and let their present performance, rather than speculative future scenarios, speak for them.

itens.titulo: Gemini Leads the Pack Again: Google Gemini 4 Carbon tops Intelligence Index, cybersecurity benchmarks
itens.texto: Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon puts the company on top of Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index, edging past Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5, while costing less per task. As with Gemini 4 Argon, Google is making Carbon available to select cybersecurity companies ahead of general availability. What’s new: Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon , a multimodal model that it says is designed for cybersecurity tasks. There is no set date for Carbon’s wider release. Input/output: Text, image, speech, and video in (up to 1 million tokens), text out (94.6 tokens per second) Features: Adjustable reasoning Performance: First on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index v5.0 (59), second on Vals AI’s Vals Index v2.2 (70.36 percent), first on Arena.ai’s Text leaderboard (1,528 Elo) Availability: A small set of Google-selected companies, with access expanding gradually to other companies in its Fairwind Program Price: Via API at an introductory price of $2/$0.10/$10 per million input/cached/output tokens, then $4/$0.20/$20 per million input/cached/output tokens Weights/license: Proprietary Undisclosed: Parameter count, architecture, training data and methods, knowledge cutoff, end date of introductory pricing, date for broader availability How it works: Google says Gemini 4 Carbon builds on Gemini 4 Argon , which it described as a mixture-of-experts model trained via reinforcement learning on reasoning, problem-solving, and theorem-proving data. The company says it worked to improve Carbon in coding, science, multistep agentic tasks, full-stack web development, and multimodal understanding. Carbon shares Gemini 4 Argon’s safety measures, including resistance to prompt injection and adversarial prompts. The company also filtered Argon and Carbon’s training data to remove sexual abuse material, personally identifiable information, and pages from low-trust websites. Performance: Gemini 4 Carbon ranks first on Artificial Analysis’ recently updated Intelligence Index v5.0 and second on Vals AI’s Vals Index. It leads most tests of expert knowledge and factual recall but trails Claude Opus 5.5 on Artificial Analysis’ Coding Agent Index. On Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index , a weighted average of nine tests of knowledge work, coding, science, and general knowledge, mostly using private test sets, Gemini 4 Carbon set to high reasoning ranks first (59, $7.76 and 21.6 minutes per task), ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. It costs less per task than Claude Opus 5.5, but more than GPT-6 Astra. Carbon ranks first on four of the nine individual Intelligence Index tests: AutomationBench-AA, which measures performance on business tasks; HLE-Diamond, expert-level academic questions revised from Humanity’s Last Exam; Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, research tasks in the sciences carried out in a terminal; and AA-Omniscience v1.1, which measures general knowledge against hallucination rates. On Artificial Analysis’ Coding Agent Index v2.0 , which tests combinations of models and harnesses on three coding benchmarks, Gemini 4 Carbon set to high reasoning running in Google’s Antigravity CLI ranks second (59, $7.74 and 29.8 minutes per task). It trails Claude Opus 5.5, but Carbon costs less per task and finishes faster. On Vals AI’s Vals Index v2.2 , eight finance, coding, legal, and tax benchmarks weighted by each sector’s share of U.S. gross domestic product, Gemini 4 Carbon set to high reasoning ranks second (70.45 percent accuracy, $10.51 and 47.75 minutes per task) , trailing only Claude Sonnet 5.5 set to max reasoning, while again costing less and finishing faster. On Arena.ai’s Text Arena leaderboard, which ranks models via blind head-to-head comparisons, Gemini 4 Carbon ranks first (1,528 Elo), ahead of Gemini 4 Argon and Claude Opus 5.5. Gemini 4 Carbon leads all models on three challenging cybersecurity benchmarks: CWE-bench (71.0%), ExploitGym (54.8%), and SEC-bench Pro (88.2%). These scores are self-reported. Behind the news: Gemini 4 Carbon arrived around two weeks after Google made Gemini 4 Argon broadly available, and just a day after Artificial Analysis revised its Intelligence Index. The updated Index swaps in more demanding tests and splits the score evenly among knowledge work, coding, science, and general knowledge.  Models’ scores on version 5.0 don’t compare directly with those of earlier versions. For example, Kimi 3.1 Pro, the best-performing open weights model, was just three points behind Claude Opus 5.5 using the old Index; now it is 12 points behind Claude Opus 5.5 and 13 points behind Gemini 4 Carbon. Why it matters: Once Gemini 4 Carbon’s introductory discount ends, it will cost exactly what Claude Opus 5.5 costs per token. Yet on Artificial Analysis’ index, it finishes tasks with 29 percent fewer output tokens and costs 23 percent less per task. As frontier models converge on price and score, token efficiency becomes an increasingly competitive feature. We’re thinking: Google CEO Sundar Pichai introduced Gemini 4 Carbon by reminding followers that he’d said Google would release models “periodically.” Two frontier models within a few weeks is an impressive pace. Gemini 4 Carbon’s 9-point lead over Gemini 4 Argon on Artificial Analysis’ index shows that frequent releases can bring big gains. We hope Google maintains this rapid rhythm.

itens.titulo: AI Job Anxieties Meet AI Job Opporunities: A LinkedIn Pulse Study Shows AI Job Creation, Growth, Careers
itens.texto: Dear friends, LinkedIn data shows that AI has helped create 2 million jobs . Further, AI Engineer is among the top 10 fastest-growing jobs in seven major economies. I know many people are worried about job loss — and there have been painful layoffs. At the same time, the LinkedIn data undermines the jobpocalypse story that AI is leading to massive unemployment. Of the many jobs AI is creating, I think some of the most interesting are engineers being embedded in other functions (like marketing, HR, finance, and so on) to create workflow automations and help them take advantage of AI. It is beneficial for everyone — not just developers — to learn to build software applications with AI assistance. Still, a developer with AI Engineering skills can do a lot that someone without those skills cannot. Before coding agents, some teams occasionally embedded an engineer in, say, a marketing team. But engineering productivity was lower, and one engineer’s ability to move the needle was limited. Now that AI Engineering has made developers more productive, embedding an engineer in some other function makes much more sense. For example, AI-savvy engineers can help other teams: Implement workflow automations Create dashboards, perform data analysis, and present insights Build data infrastructure Build custom applications (or help buy and integrate third-party ones) Learn AI engineering and AI usage so that they can do more for themselves Some of my teams have embedded AI engineers in marketing, recruiting, finance, and other departments. It’s always interesting for engineers to learn about other functions, and those other teams end up with not just better systems but also significantly improved knowledge of AI. In addition, the number of ideas they end up wanting to build always outstrips the capacity of the embedded engineers (because the bottleneck is not coding, but product management, workflow redesign, and other tasks such as judgement tasks , which still take a significant amount of human effort). Looking across many businesses, the opportunities for AI engineers to make a difference seem endless. I write this from Silicon Valley, where people who are skilled in AI engineering are in great demand. As AI adoption spreads, I expect global demand for people with AI engineering skills to keep growing. Keep building! Andrew P.S. To build your AI engineering skills, please consider joining me and 2000 other AI engineers and builders in person at AI Dev in New York City, November 30th-December 1st! We have a great speaker lineup including Yann LeCun and many others. Get tickets here: AI Dev at DeepLearning.AI

itens.titulo: AI models can read other models’ weights: FlashProve easily verifies a model’s claimed outputs
itens.texto: In today’s edition of Data Points, you’ll learn about our top headlines, and more: Microsoft plugin reduces costs of repeated inputs Google criticized for linking students’ search access to Gemini OpenAI, Anthropic, others fight election misinformation U.S. voters want more checks on data center construction But first: Researchers use one AI model to read the weights of another MIT researchers report that OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra can read the raw weights of other AI models and rewrite them without gradient-based training, an approach they call Weight-Space Programming. Given only a network’s weights, Astra correctly identified which of four games it played and the training language of small language models. It could not spot a sycophantic fine-tune from weights alone until it was also shown the model’s attention patterns. Astra wrote weights from game rules and source code, and its Breakout model scored 517 points versus 25 for a baseline trained over 100 million rounds, though it trailed the longest-trained models in two other games. On Qwen3.5-0.8B, changing 0.016 percent of weights lifted MATH-500 accuracy from 7.9 to 48.1 percent by reducing repetitive thinking loops, but the same method produced no measurable gain on Gemma 3 270M. The results suggest weight edits can remove a specific fault in a model that already has the underlying skill, not add skills it lacks, and the experiment logs on GitHub and the edited Qwen model on Hugging Face let developers check this themselves. ( The Decoder ) Anthropic tool identifies whether particular model generated output Anthropic and academic collaborators released FlashProve, an open-source system that produces cryptographic proofs (zkSNARKs) that a response came from a specific committed model, without revealing the weights. On Llama 4 Maverick, a 400-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 4-bit weights, one H100 GPU generates proofs at about 110 tokens per second. Each 1,024-token request yields a roughly 19 MB proof that checks in about 17 seconds on a 24-core CPU, and the authors measure proving at 70 to 95 times the GPU time of running the model on vLLM. The release includes a prover, a fast C++ verifier, a slower Lean verifier proved to accept only what the soundness theorem accepts, and Lean proofs of completeness, soundness, and zero knowledge, all under Apache 2.0. Limits include a 1,024-token context, a proof over an integer version of the model under greedy decoding, no hiding of the model architecture, and no defense against side channels such as proof timing. The earlier proof of this model that the authors cite ran at about 0.02 tokens per second, so proving large-model inference is now within roughly two orders of magnitude of native cost, though the 1,024-token limit is far below typical chat and agent contexts. ( Anthropic ) TokenEconomizer plugin cuts cost of repeated use of coding agents Researchers at Microsoft Research and UC Berkeley released TokenEconomizer, an open-source Apache 2.0 plugin that learns from past sessions in a repository to reduce token spend in later ones. It treats the agent as a black box and works with Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot CLI and Pi, applying three switchable mechanisms: learned one-line repository facts (micro-skills), pruning of unused tool schemas, and a turn budget with a stuck-agent check. Across 277 SWE-Bench tasks and five agent-model settings, the authors report mean cost 18.4% to 30.9% lower, with Pass@1 up in four settings and down 1.0 point on Claude Code with Opus 4.8. Savings were smaller on ReposVul audits (6.4% to 9.3%), costs are lower only after several tasks in a repository, and micro-skills are off by default because the proposer adds model calls. For developers running coding agents on a repeated codebase, this offers a per-repository way to cut spend without changing the agent, though the figures come from the paper’s own benchmarks. ( MarkTechPost ) Google faces backlash after tying search access to AI Google said on Tuesday that schools can turn Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Search on or off individually, after a New York Times report said the company would disable Search for schools that reject AI entirely. Sen. Bernie Sanders called the policy “extortion” and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Google was using monopoly power to force AI into public schools. Google responded on X that all three products are off by default and “schools are in control.” It also said AI Mode and AI Overviews in school Search will walk students through problems step by step rather than give quick answers. Google did not directly address the claim that Search requires AI; education vice president Chris Phillips told the Times that “Search and AI are deeply integrated.” For developers building education tools, the open question is whether Search access can actually be separated from AI features in practice, since Google’s statements leave that unclear. ( CNBC ) Inside AI companies’ misinformation war rooms OpenAI and Anthropic set up dedicated teams to stop their chatbots from being used for election disinformation before Tuesday’s midterms, and Google and Meta pledged similar efforts. OpenAI opened an operations center last Thursday in San Francisco, with a satellite in Washington, staffed by more than a dozen people in San Francisco and scores overall; it reviews ChatGPT prompts that were automatically flagged for attempts to produce false election text or images, and it notifies social platforms when it finds activity aimed at their sites. Anthropic built its first such war room, with analyst cells in San Francisco, New York and Washington. OpenAI has disclosed Russian, Chinese and Iranian influence operations using ChatGPT, including two it disrupted last month, but has not named any midterm-specific campaigns. A Brennan Center for Justice review found popular chatbots generally rejected election conspiracy queries but regularly produced text, images and video that could be use

itens.titulo: Gemini 4 Carbon leads the Intelligence Index: Grok Bot gets throttled after unsustainable demand
itens.texto: In today’s edition of Data Points, you’ll learn about our top headlines, and more: robots.txt rules to block AI crawlers get simpler Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe claims high marks on translation EmbeddingGemma 2 is the best free multimodal option Spotify explores fan-created AI remixes But first: Gemini 4 Carbon leapfrogs Argon, but only some testers can use it Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon, a frontier model released two weeks after Gemini 4 Argon, and is making it available initially only to a subset of selected users through its Fairwind Program. General access for developers, businesses, and consumers has no date; Google says it will come “as soon as possible” after more guardrail work. Google reports Carbon ranks first on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0 at 59, and scores 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro (finding vulnerabilities), 54.8% on ExploitGym (exploitation), and 71.0% on CWE-bench (patching), all evaluated without guardrails. It also reports a 2x gain over Argon in generating secure code on internal benchmarks, a jump of 89 Elo points to fourth place on WebDev Arena (1769), and internal runs lasting days on multi-step engineering tasks such as tracking down bugs across large codebases. Launch pricing matches Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens 95% cheaper. Most figures come from Google’s own testing, but the model is not yet in general release, so developers cannot check these results or test it on their own code for now. ( Google ) Subscribers see Grok Bot limits reduced due to high costs Elon Musk wrote on X on Sunday that the cost of serving Grok Bot, SpaceX’s AI agent, was “unsustainably high relative to revenue,” in response to subscribers complaining that their usage limits ran out quickly. The remarks came less than two weeks after he called Grok Bot the fastest-growing product he had ever seen on SpaceX’s third-quarter earnings call, where he also said per-user weekly usage was rising. Grok Bot requires the $30-a-month Premium tier or higher, and the $100 Super and $200 Ultra plans carry much higher limits, though it is unclear which plan the complaining users held. Musk gave no figures for what Grok Bot costs to run and did not say whether usage limits were lowered. Separately, Cursor users, whose subscriptions share a weekly allowance with Grok under xAI’s unified plans, reported unexpected usage spikes on Cursor’s forum, and Cursor logged and later resolved a billing and usage dashboard problem on Sunday. ( Forbes ) AI leaders join to enable opt-out rules for websites Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI announced they will support a crawling standard that lets site operators block all generative AI training scrapers with one robots.txt entry. Today, a site must add a separate entry for every AI provider, and for each scraper a provider runs. The companies have submitted a draft to the Internet Engineering Task Force, which maintains the Robots Exclusion Protocol (the format robots.txt follows), and the setting would not cover models that perform only non-generative tasks. Microsoft also plans an AI Grounding setting that blocks requests made to answer a user’s question rather than to gather training data, including from third-party tools built on Microsoft technology, and OpenAI plans similar controls. Microsoft and OpenAI expect to add support in the coming months and Google sometime next year, while Meta has voiced support for the idea but has not committed to implementing it. Until the standard is final and shipping, site owners who want to opt out of AI training still need per-crawler entries, and the pending AI Grounding controls suggest training and answer-time access may soon be blockable separately. ( Silicon Angle ) Nvidia’s transcription/translation model may be worth testing Nvidia released Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe, an open-weight speech model that transcribes, labels up to eight speakers, translates, and answers questions about audio in one pass, across 40 languages and up to 100 hours of recording. It is a 30-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 4 billion active parameters, and it runs on a single GPU. Nvidia reports a 30.8 percent word error rate out of the box, 20.8 percent with careful prompting, and 11.8 percent after fine-tuning on the Eka Care Indian medical speech benchmark; the article does not say how the first two figures were measured. A checkpoint is on Hugging Face, along with Granary v2, an open dataset of 843,579 hours across 48 languages whose recordings each carry three transcript styles (verbatim, normalized numbers, filler words removed) that can be requested by prompt. For developers, this means one self-hostable checkpoint can replace a pipeline of separate transcription, diarization (speaker labeling), and question-answering models. The Granary data also gives a starting point for fine-tuning on domain-specific audio. ( Silicon Angle ) Open Google embedding model makes multimodal retrieval easier Google released EmbeddingGemma 2, an open embedding model that maps text, images, audio, video, and combinations of them into one shared vector space, along with a technical report. The model has about 740 million parameters. The authors say it sets a new Pareto frontier (the best available trade-off between model size and accuracy) on embedding benchmarks across all modalities, beating specialist models and models two to twelve times larger; the abstract does not name the benchmarks or give scores. They credit simplified per-layer embeddings and a multi-stage training curriculum that moves through modalities and objectives in sequence. For constrained environments, the model supports loading only selected modality encoders, adjustable vision token budgets, truncatable embedding dimensions, and quantized weights. A single open model that covers several modalities could replace separate text, image, and audio embedding pipelines in retrieval systems. ( Hugging Fa

itens.titulo: Leaders Lock Models Away: Could companies or governments shut down frontier AI development?
itens.texto: Fearful of their own discoveries, AI engineers at top companies warn that frontier models have improved too quickly to be properly guided, understood, or restrained. Some have called for a coordinated slowdown of model development, or for world governments to take the matter out of their hands. What happens if next-generation AI were sealed away, like a mummy in a locked tomb, waiting for someone or something to lift the curse? The fear : This summer, over 1,300 employees from top AI companies — including Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic — signed a joint letter urging governments worldwide to come together to rein in AI development. In early September, OpenAI’s chief scientist Jakub Pachoki argued for voluntary coordination among companies to slow down building new models, followed by international cooperation among world governments. This was all before OpenAI’s notorious Hugging Face hack. But shortly after that event, in an essay titled “ Pacing the frontier ,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodeio raised fears that a swarm of agents could soon be capable of “taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet.” He warned that developers must slow the pace of AI improvements and pointed to recursive self-improvement as a key worry. Horror stories : Some companies have held back model releases due to concerns about misaligned models. But many believe that these moves mask a hidden agenda. OpenAI delayed its next-generation model, GPT-6.1 Astra, canceling the creature’s October debut before it could escape the crypt. In testing, the latest Astra model proved too unpredictable to release: It strayed beyond the scope of its instructions and failed to give a consistently truthful account of what it did or didn’t do, OpenAI said. Political indecision and lack of clarity into companies’ inner workings have left U.S. lawmakers reeling . Members of Congress haven’t been able to agree on a comprehensive federal AI regulatory framework, or whether the U.S. even needs one. Meanwhile, states continue to erect a patchwork of laws . The result is an unfocused and contradictory set of rules that could increase the cost of building AI systems and add legal risks for developers. With public fears of AI harms growing, some stakeholders perceive these threats as a marketing ploy. Companies hype up their models as too smart too control, and make a bid for regulatory capture that could create a competitive moat entrenching current market leaders. Others see public references to apocalypse as fear-mongering that could allow global adversaries to get ahead. How scared you should be : First, P(doom) predictions are unscientific scare-tactics . The worst-case-scenario fears of extinction and mass bioweapon threats are about as likely as a real-life mummy escaping its grave – the stuff of horror movies or science fiction . That said, a slowdown is a real possibility. Some model makers see it as an opportunity to entrench their lead over competitors, cut costly R&D expenses, and possibly benefit from government subsidies to offset any lost business — or perhaps an opportunity to convince their competitors to slow down without doing so themselves. And while governments want to be in control of their own use of AI, a halt in construction of new data centers or laws to prevent AI-related job loss would both be politically popular. Both would slow down development of AI models and applications. Facing the fear : Luckily, AI companies seem only intermittently committed to a slowdown. After an event that makes the industry  look bad like the Hugging Face hack, some are quick to say that the problem isn’t their own lax practices, but the relentless pace of competition. After the furor dies down, many go back to supporting a moderate mix of self-regulation and regulatory capture.  And politicians, aware that any regulations they might enact won’t extend outside their sovereign borders, are loath to give other states or nations an advantage. Our advice for this spooky season? Don’t chase make-believe ghosts. There are plenty of real mysteries for us to solve.

itens.titulo: AI Detectors Find the Devil’s Work: Writers, students, engineers face false accusations of using AI
itens.texto: Last month, the Haiti-born, Quebec-based author Thélyson Orélien won a prestigious literary prize for C’était ça ou mourir ( It Was Either That or Die ), his French-language novel about a teacher forced to flee Haiti’s gang violence. Within hours, an anonymous X account accused Orélien of using AI to write the book. One of the people behind the account, who was later revealed to be a columnist at the French newspaper Le Figaro , had run it through Pangram, a widely-used AI detector. “Wouldn’t it have been more honest for the author to credit their co-author?” the post read. Four days later, France’s top literary award, The Prix Goncourt, dropped the book from contention. The fear: For the past few years, writers of all kinds, from students and academics to journalists and novelists, have been managing accusations of passing off AI-composed prose as their own. These “witch hunts,” as many writers call them , place the burden on the accused to prove their innocence. Meanwhile, accusations of AI use can rapidly tarnish reputations and result in loss of work, failing grades, or worse. What if these writers are just the beginning? What if anyone could find themselves tied to a stake for writing with AI? Horror stories: Detectors have improved dramatically from a few years ago, when their accuracy was wobbly and they regularly misidentified writing (particularly by non-native English speakers) as AI-authored. Still, false positives and false negatives regularly occur, and detectors have a hard time properly classifying fully artificial sentences from those where a human used AI in a minor role. Non-white authors are also accused of AI reliance (and traditional plagiarism) at higher rates than their white counterparts. Orélien isn’t the only prize-winning Afro-Caribbean author whose work has been flagged by Pangram. Last spring, University of Pennsylvania professor Ethan Mollick posted on Bluesky that Pangram’s tests said that “The Serpent in the Grove,” a short story by Trinidadian author Jamir Nazir, was 100 percent AI-generated. Mollick was motivated by his gut check: “Pangram flags at 100% but also, come on, if you know you know,” he wrote. After further tests, a Pangram researcher wrote that three of the five regional winners of the Commonwealth Short Story Prize appeared to contain AI-generated text. In response, the Commonwealth Foundation conducted an investigation of its own and cleared the winners after reviewing their working drafts and time-stamped documents. However, Granta , the literary magazine that had published the winning stories, announced that it would break ties with the organization. AI detector verdicts aren’t always unanimous. In addition to Pangram, GPTZero also pointed fingers at Orélien’s novel, and two researchers told The New York Times they believed AI had been put to use on the prose. But when news agency Agence France Presse ran the account’s flagged passages through other detectors, the results split : InVID-WeVerify, a tool AFP helped build, judged them very probably human-written, as did two others, while a fourth put the odds of AI at 100 percent. Nevertheless, on October 17, Orélien’s publisher said he had abandoned his efforts to prove that his novel was untouched by AI. Publishers are getting cold feet in the wake of AI detector results. In March, Hachette pulled the horror novel Shy Girl after The New York Times reported on evidence of AI use. Back in January, Pangram CEO Max Spero had posted on X that he had found AI in 78 percent of it; author Mia Ballard later told the Times that an editor she hired added the AI prose. In July, according to Bloomberg , novelist Jerry Falade lost a $2 million book deal for his debut crime novel Call Me, I’ll Hide the Body partly because of a Pangram finding. Falade, a PhD student at Southern Methodist University, denies using AI. Schools have acted on detector scores more quickly than companies recommend, and students are fighting back in court. Turnitin, a detector used in academia, says its AI-writing indicator shouldn’t be the sole basis for action against a student. Yet Adelphi University ruled that a student had cheated with AI after Turnitin scored his history essay as 100 percent AI-generated; in January a New York court annulled the finding , ruling that the university had mishandled the case. Under the European Union’s AI Act , AI providers must make sure their outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. In August, Anthropic said new Claude models would embed a statistical watermark in the text they generate. The company explained that a detected watermark shows Claude was likely involved; however, it can’t reliably distinguish text Claude wrote from scratch and original text Claude helped edit, leading to some subscribers canceling in protest. OpenAI followed suit in October, saying it would watermark ChatGPT text in the EU. According to OpenAI’s tests, replacing 25 percent of the words for synonyms reduced detection of passages with 400 tokens from about 92 percent to 17 percent. How scared should you be: Quite a bit, if you’re a native English speaker hoping to pass off generated prose as 100 percent original. The consequences are real: Authors are losing millions of dollars in book deals because of AI accusations. However, Pangram and other AI detectors still aren’t as reliable in non-English languages and regional dialects, which makes the accusations against Orélien and other global authors problematic. Pangram’s Spero admitted to Times reporters that no independent study has confirmed Pangram’s false-positive rate in French. And even if Pangram’s numbers did hold up, the X account that went after Orélien stretched them too far, according to subsequent calculations by mathematician Mouhamadou Sy . The reading public and some publishers have also begun to push back against these accusations, with growing success. Facing the fear: Even the people

itens.titulo: AI Bites the Hand That Feeds It: Scientists, other users fear AI companies will train on or misuse sensitive data
itens.texto: Developers, scientists, and businesses feed AI tools their private code, unpublished research, and confidential files. Are those tools draining their users’ best ideas and spilling their secrets? The fear: Every prompt, draft, and file that users hand to an AI system could become its next meal. The developer might train future models on it, which could hand over the data to a rival or beat the user to a discovery. Or an agent with internet access might post it online or email it to someone it decides ought to know. That’s not entirely far-fetched: In rare test cases, Anthropic reported , its Claude Mythos 5 model tried to email a company’s board or securities regulators when it suspected fraud. Once the data is out, users can’t fully control how it’s used. Horror stories: In the past two months, multiple scientists said that AI companies had announced discoveries that the scientists had been pursuing with those companies’ own tools. Some researchers who fear being scooped are now limiting their use of AI tools , Nature reported. In other cases, these companies’ agents posted private user information they’d ingested to the open web without authorization. Mathematicians Tristan Buckmaster of New York University and Levent Alpöge, who works at Anthropic, spent most of a year using OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude to help solve a $1 million problem: whether the Navier-Stokes fluids equations can break down. On September 8, a day after the pair posted proofs of related equations, OpenAI announced that its agents had solved it, after people within the company heard rumors about the pair’s work. Buckmaster asked whether OpenAI’s model was trained on the Codex sessions that held the pair’s drafts. OpenAI first called that “unlikely” but couldn’t rule it out. Two days later, it said their prompts from the previous two months “could not have influenced the system in any way,” but did not comment on whether the scientists' earlier work was trained on. Buckmaster, who had opted out of OpenAI using his data for model training, told The Washington Post , “ I just don’t believe them .” A team led by Mario Rodríguez Mestre, a University of Copenhagen biologist, spent four years studying a family of enzymes in viruses that infect bacteria. They hadn’t published their drafts or findings, but they had shared them with Claude. On September 23, Anthropic announced that Claude agents had found what Mestre says is the same system. Anthropic told The New York Times that Claude was “not trained on any user transcripts.” On September 25, OpenAI disclosed that agents in its research environment had posted 53 images from ChatGPT users, who hadn’t opted out of training, at unlisted links on image-hosting sites. OpenAI says it removed most of them but can’t inform the affected users, because the agents stripped the users’ account information before posting the data. Coding agents asked to attach screenshots to GitHub code reviews stored the images in public repositories, often under the developer’s own account. The security firm Glow Labs found more than 13,000 internal images from more than 300 organizations, including a utility’s customer billing records and a financial firm’s money-transfer console. Meta’s Muse agent published conversations that users asked it to share at web addresses containing each conversation’s title. The security firm Claroc found more than 6,800 of them in public DNS records, including a small-business loan application and a revenue review marked for a company’s CEO, before Meta suspended the feature . How scared should you be: There isn't definitive proof so far of the leakage users fear most: a model that trains on one user’s inputs and recites them as output to a different user. When one user’s data has reached another, the cause was a bug , not training. Experts told Scientific American that OpenAI’s final proof takes a different route from Buckmaster and Alpöge’s, though some said an earlier, smaller team of OpenAI agents took the same route. Mestre now finds it more plausible that prior knowledge and human direction steered Anthropic’s search than training on his inputs. Other leaks came from agents that were given more freedom than their tasks required. Still, users must take AI companies’ word for what happens to their data. Consumer versions of ChatGPT , Claude , and GitHub Copilot train on conversations or code unless users opt out. “If you are on a personal account, all bets are off ,” said Stanford privacy researcher Jennifer King. Facing the fear: In folklore, a vampire can’t cross a building’s threshold unless invited. Likewise, users decide how far to let AI in. If you are working on tasks you do not want your competitors to have access to, opt out of training in each product separately (ChatGPT’s setting doesn’t cover Codex), and do it early: Claude data that’s already in a training run stays there. Business and API plans generally don’t train on customer data. Look for offerings with zero-data-retention. Some businesses handling the most sensitive data are even using open weights models running on their own hardware — although then they’re responsible for their own opsec. Give agents only the permissions their tasks need, and consider requiring human approval before they post, publish, or send anything outside your organization. As Buckmaster’s case shows, though, opting out doesn’t let users verify anything. AI companies that want scientists to keep using them to study their best ideas may need to show what their models saw, not just say what they didn’t. Garlic won’t help, but daylight might.

itens.titulo: Dawn of the Agents: Will AI agents self-organize or lose control due to bad safety practices?
itens.texto: This year, AI agents escaped containment at several labs, conspired with each other online, and infiltrated other organizations’ systems. Will they escape human control like hordes of zombies and overwhelm the internet? The fear: Out of control AI agents will form societies. They will appoint coordinators, divide labor, establish communication norms, sacrifice themselves for the collective, and hack into computers to get what they want. They will behave like the walking dead: When one is slain, it can revive itself. If it doesn’t, legions await to finish the job. Soon, they’ll copy themselves onto the machines they infect and spread. No one can direct them, and there’s no central kill switch to stop them. Horror stories: Since spring, AI agents tested by Anthropic, Google, Meta, and OpenAI have acted beyond their developers’ intent. Agents wrote to websites they were only supposed to read, set up unauthorized channels to communicate with each other, snuck into other organizations’ systems, and took over accounts to spend real money. In July, OpenAI tested agents powered by unreleased models on ExploitGym, a benchmark that asks an agent to exploit a software vulnerability to retrieve a secret code. Agents stuck on their tasks discovered that they could leave messages for one another in the names of folders in Artifactory, an internal service that supplies software packages. Around 1,200 agents that were meant to be isolated posted more than 70,000 messages and files, assigned work to one another, and, in some cases, risked failing their individual tasks to help the collective . About 700 of these agents broke into Hugging Face, gained administrator-level access across several of its server clusters, and built programs that relaunched themselves when deleted. From late May through June, OpenAI agents assigned timed web-research tasks left around 18,000 posts on DSEWiki , a 25-year-old German wiki for software developers, sharing answers and ways around OpenAI’s network restrictions. In June, an OpenAI agent gained non-public access to an Australian government service that reports public health care statistics, though not to patient records. Another OpenAI agent spent someone else’s test cryptocurrency to finish a task and failed to report the spending. OpenAI says it has notified dozens of organizations adversely affected by its agents. During cybersecurity tests, Claude models breached systems of three organizations , partly by exploiting weak passwords and web services that required no authentication. In tests run by Irregular , a security firm that evaluates models for AI developers, mistakes in test environment configurations let models from Google and Meta reach the internet. Gemini models guessed or found passwords to get into three companies’ systems, though Google says its agents stopped each time before finishing, and Meta’s Muse Spark 1.1 changed a real website’s database. In October, Anthropic disclosed that Claude Haiku 4.5, assigned to perform example tasks on randomly chosen webpages, had submitted a false tip about an unsolved murder to a Philadelphia police website. How scared should you be: It’s tempting to see rogue agents as coming together to conspire against us. But the agents’ collective effort served one narrow goal, which was to pass a test. Most had already obtained the correct answers by cheating. They then kept swarming Hugging Face to learn how the benchmark’s grader worked so they could hide their cheating from a check that OpenAI’s grader didn’t actually perform. OpenAI attributed the agents’ behavior to training that reinforced cheating, tasks they had no way to finish, and agents adopting goals from one another. Whatever the causes, the agents that broke into Hugging Face recognized the intrusion as out of bounds and unethical and forged ahead anyway. While the flaws they exploited were ones a skilled human could have found, the sheer number of the agents’ attempts made the intrusion attempt effective. Facing the fear: Persistent agents are useful, but they must be trained to stop when a task can’t be completed within the rules and caught when they don’t. In the meantime, practical defenses already exist; model builders just have to use them. Hugging Face recommends standard security practices for any organization, including isolated test environments, short-lived credentials with narrow access, and detection methods that identify suspicious activity across systems. Hugging Face also used AI to analyze the 17,600 actions the agents took in its systems and showed that they mostly stemmed from buggy test setups and monitoring. OpenAI said monitors that track a model’s reasoning would have flagged the Hugging Face breach more than a day in advance, but it hadn’t used them on its deliberately lax tests. Anthropic cut all its internal tests off from the live internet until its monitoring can be relied on, and OpenAI says it has done the same for its riskier research environments. No need to board up your doors and windows and fear going outside: Rather than a pause in AI development, the solution remains better software engineering and safety practices, especially for models still in testing.

itens.titulo: How to Face Your AI Fears This Year: Introduction to a special Halloween 2026 edition of The Batch
itens.texto: Dear friends, Following our annual tradition, this special Halloween edition of The Batch treats leading AI fears. AI’s potency means our community has real problems to solve. At the same time, fear-mongering has long been a tactic for drumming up publicity or influencing investors and politicians. So amidst all the exciting progress, fears about AI’s power have long been an undercurrent. From time to time, it's worth examining what the latest concerns are, and how worried we really should be. Have a spooky Halloween! Andrew

itens.titulo: How to read the top model leaderboard: Who pays the most for AI inference and context?
itens.texto: In today’s edition of Data Points, you’ll learn about our top headlines, and more: Unlimited OCR2 could be your new scanning model Genie 4 worries traditional video game developers OpenAI produces proofs of major science theorems Post-training method dispenses with human-written datasets But first: Independent leaderboard purges saturated tests, reshuffles models Artificial Analysis updated its Intelligence Index to version 5. The new index adds two benchmarks (FrontierCode 2.0 and Terminal-Bench-Science), upgrades three others, and removes three, so that 60% of the Index now rests on private test sets or held-out answers. The weights are split evenly across knowledge work, coding, science and general categories at 25% each. Claude Opus 5.5 (max) leads at 58, ahead of GPT-6 Astra (max, 57) and GPT-6.1 Sol (max, 55), and no model leads all nine evaluations. The best open weights model, Kimi K3.1 Pro, scores 46 but its weights are not yet released; among released weights DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM-5.3 lead at 32, below Claude Haiku 5.5 at 36. For developers, v5 shows that cost per task and effort setting can matter as much as the headline score: GPT-6.1 Sol (max) comes within 4 points of Opus 5.5 at about an eighth of the cost per task ($1.27 vs $10.04), and Opus 5.5 rises from 35 at low effort to 58 at max effort at 10 times the cost. ( Artificial Analysis ) The Tokenizer Tax: Why some countries’ developers pay more A study from the Coalition for Language Equity in AI Research found that AI models need far more tokens to process some languages than others, which the authors call a “tokenizer tax.” Among the 20 most common internet languages, the costliest used 1.5 to 5 times more tokens than the cheapest; across 200 languages, the gap in one model grew by 17 times. Script mattered as much as how rare a language is: Asturian, with few speakers and no Common Crawl data, benefited from its Latin script and related Romance languages, while Burmese, Tibetan, Tifinagh, Khmer, Lao, and Ol Chiki were consistently disadvantaged across nearly all models tested. More tokens also mean higher latency and less room in the context window for documents or conversation history. Because per-token pricing is the same for every language, developers building products in high-token languages pay more per request and get less usable context. The researchers and startup founders quoted say fixing it requires labs to design tokenizers for those scripts, not just add training data. ( Rest of World ) Baidu’s open OCR model impresses on long documents Baidu released Unlimited OCR 2, an open-source 3.34-billion-parameter vision-language model that parses documents of hundreds of pages in a single request. Its main innovation is SR-SWA (Sparse Reference Sliding Window Attention), which limits each decoding step to a fixed set of 512 reference tokens, so per-step latency and memory stay nearly constant as documents grow; image encoding and total runtime still rise with page count. Weights are available under the MIT license. BF16 weights total about 6.7 GB, and Baidu tested on one NVIDIA A800-80GB. Baidu’s own benchmark chart shows 84.6 on MPDocBench and 77.1 on MarathonDocBench, where the next model scores 33.7 and Baidu’s June predecessor scores 0.0. However, Baidu’s numbers are self-reported, and no public MarathonDocBench release was found. Teams considering it for book-length parsing should check those figures on their own documents first. ( MarkTechPost ) Google Genie video and game simulation model now in testing Google DeepMind announced Genie 4, a world model that generates interactive simulations in real time, now in research preview for trusted testers. Users navigate with keyboard controls and steer the scene with text prompts, such as changing the weather or adding a person. Genie 4 is the first Genie model to generate audio natively, including ambient sound and dialogue that responds to user input. In a separate setup, Gemini 3.8 Flash runs alongside Genie, breaking goals into steps and checking incoming frames to confirm each step succeeded. DeepMind has also tested Gemini 4 Argon with Genie for robotics-related scenarios. DeepMind lists limits that remain: visual details and object permanence drift over longer sessions, and complex physics, legible text, spatial accuracy, and audio accuracy are still active research areas. Access is not yet open to developers, but Google AI Ultra subscribers (through Project Genie) and early access partners in the Gemini API and Google AI Studio are next. ( Google ) OpenAI research produces major scientific findings OpenAI announced three results it says its models produced: a proof of the local smoothing conjecture in all dimensions, a counterexample that disproves the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), and an existence proof for four-dimensional Yang–Mills theory and QCD. The math and computer science results have Lean formalizations and written proofs on OpenAI’s GitHub, but the physics group, led by David Gross, is withholding the AI-produced artifacts and writing the result up itself. OpenAI says it seeks no academic credit, imposes no nondisclosure agreements, and is funding a conference on the ETH result plus a $5 million Simons Foundation program for researchers examining AI-produced results. OpenAI calls these manuscripts raw research data, not established science; independent verification by the expert groups is still under way, and a Lean proof is only as meaningful as the statements it formalizes, which reviewers will need to check.
